rules: Registration with general boundaries is sufficient for the majority of registered titles.
The two main routes to greater boundary precision are a boundary agreement or a determined boundary.
A boundary agreement can address the legal boundary position, maintenance of a boundary feature, or both.
A recorded boundary agreement does not itself convert the registered boundary from general to determined.
A determined boundary shows the exact line of the boundary of a registered estate.
HM Land Registry records an already identified exact line; the procedure is not itself a mechanism for resolving a neighbour dispute.
The affected title plans show the general position, while the filed determined-boundary plan is retained to identify the exact line.
An owner may be unable to obtain determined status if the evidence does not establish the exact line.
The exact line must be identified by a plan or by a plan combined with a verbal description.
The plan must include enough surrounding physical features to locate the boundary's general position on Ordnance Survey mapping.
All owners of land adjoining the boundary and an address for service for each must be identified.
Adjoining red edging on two title plans does not exclude the possibility that a third party owns intervening land such as a drain.
The registrar must be satisfied about exact-line identification, an arguable case for its position, and identification of adjoining owners.
Adjoining owners are normally notified unless the evidence includes their written agreement or a court order determining the line.
Supporting evidence can include deed plans or provisions, statutory declarations, statements of truth, signed statements and expert reports.
An expert's finding may bind the instructing parties but is not conclusive for the registrar's arguable-case assessment.
A chartered land surveyor or other suitably qualified professional is normally recommended to prepare the determined-boundary plan.
A determined boundary is normally surveyed using measurements from permanent features or Ordnance Survey National Grid coordinates.
The plan must identify the start, end and turning points of the boundary, preferably with lettered points.
The plan must state its scale; the preferred scale is no smaller than 1:200 and the preferred sheet size is no larger than A3.
Where a boundary coincides with a physical feature, the plan must state which side or which point of that feature the line follows.
A determined-boundary plan must not contain a disclaimer such as 'for identification purposes only' that casts doubt on accuracy.
Plan measurements must be accurate to plus or minus 10mm and must be taken horizontally rather than along a slope.
Measurements must be taken from at least two defined points on permanent surrounding physical features, preferably from both sides.
Accepted National Grid coordinates require absolute accuracy of plus or minus 300mm and relative accuracy of plus or minus 10mm.
The dataset-search endpoint returns datasets filtered by supplied dataset parameters.
Dataset-search responses are available in JSON or HTML.
The dataset-search field parameter selects fields to include in the JSON response.
The dataset-search exclude_field parameter selects fields to omit from the JSON response.
The include_typologies boolean can remove typologies from dataset JSON when set to false.
A specific dataset is retrieved through the /dataset/{dataset}.{extension} endpoint.
The specific-dataset endpoint requires both the dataset identifier and a JSON-or-HTML extension.
The official OpenAPI file can be used to generate a client library for integration.
Average survey point density depends on the required resolution of the surface model.
A 1m DSM survey has an average point density of at least one point per square metre.
A 50cm surface model corresponds to an average point density of four points per square metre.
A 25cm surface model corresponds to an average point density of sixteen points per square metre.
The stated point-density targets are calculated for the DSM from last or only returns, not for the DTM.
Under vegetation, the ground points forming a 1m DTM may not reach one point per square metre.
Point density varies across the scan rather than remaining spatially uniform.
Overlap between multiple flight lines can increase local point density.
Significant terrain changes can alter point density in the forward scan direction.
A point cloud is not a regular grid, so its density must not be treated as raster resolution.
GeoPackage is being implemented gradually across the Data Services Platform as an open geospatial transfer format.
LiDAR Composite and SurfZone DEM download ZIP files now include a spatial metadata index in GeoPackage format.
The GeoPackage index describes the spatial location and temporal extent of the raster elevation data.
Technical guides associated with the metadata record describe the index format and attribute schema.
OS Terrain 50 is supplied as an online download without registration.
ASCII, GML and shapefile national supplies use 10km by 10km data tiles.
The tiled national product contains 2,858 tiles.
The tiles are arranged into 55 folders, each representing a 100km National Grid square.
GeoPackage and vector-tile formats are supplied as single national flat files.
OS Terrain 50 is maintained through annual full-tile resupply.
The annual customer supply is issued each July with revision-programme updates.
Each 10km ASCII tile contains 200 rows by 200 columns of 50m pixels.
ASCII rows progress west to east, and each following row begins 50m farther south.
ASCII height values are supplied as real values rounded to the nearest 0.1 metre.
A grid tile supply includes ASCII, GML, projection, auxiliary-style and tile-metadata files.
